summary:
West Sumatra stands under the national framework of Indonesia, a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned there for a same-sex relationship in February 2025.

West Sumatra carries no equivalent provincial religious criminal regime. The operative restrictions here are regional public-order bylaws made by city and regency authorities under Indonesia's regional-bylaw mechanism, and they bind anyone within the locality. Bukittinggi City adopted Regional Regulation (Perda) No. 2 of 2024 on Public Order, which targets LGBT people and is framed in the text as a response to local religious values and Minangkabau customs. In Limapuluh Kota regency, the regional legislature (DPRD) finalised on 13 May 2026 a draft anti-LGBT regional regulation folded into a Public Order and Tranquility (Trantibum) regulation, carrying administrative fines and rehabilitation for LGBT people.

Physical risk in Indonesia is rising. Vigilante mobs are attacking transgender people, and reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 that lists LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue: on 22 June 2025 officers raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International stated the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges; during a WhatsApp call his mother in Lima was told authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody and his mother alleges police beat him. Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment. In March 2016 the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, the government has blocked websites and apps carrying 'gay' or LGBTQ-related words including Grindr, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Document and status rules offer no cover. Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors with no third-gender or X option, legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery and a judge's approval, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Indonesia's regional-bylaw mechanism lets districts and provinces write their own public-order rules, which is how anti-LGBT restrictions have spread outside Aceh. OutRight Action International's 2022 report 'Creeping Criminalisation' mapped discriminatory national laws and regional regulations across eight provinces (Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra, Yogyakarta); West Sumatra's Bukittinggi regulation postdates that mapping, so the province appears in the spread of local anti-LGBT bylaws only through more recent instruments.

The pattern within West Sumatra runs across two separate localities in three years: a 2024 city regulation and a 2026 regency draft, both framed in religious and customary terms. Aceh remains the reference point for how far provincial religious law can go, with public caning of two men in February 2025 applied to anyone present including foreign visitors.
localsOnly:
Bukittinggi City Regional Regulation (Perda) No. 2 of 2024 on Public Order is a local instrument aimed at LGBT conduct, presented in academic analysis as an implementation of Islamic governance answering to local religious values and Minangkabau customs.

In Limapuluh Kota regency, the DPRD has taken its draft anti-LGBT provisions through to finalisation as of 13 May 2026, integrated into a Public Order and Tranquility (Trantibum) regional regulation. The draft provides for administrative fines and for rehabilitation of LGBT people, and the chair of the drafting body stated that the stages have reached finalisation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not record any arrest, prosecution or penalty actually imposed under Bukittinggi Perda No. 2 of 2024, so enforcement in practice remains unresolved.

Whether the Limapuluh Kota Ranperda has been enacted, and on what date, is not sourced here; the record establishes finalisation of the draft only. The content and legal basis of the 'rehabilitation' provision is likewise not described in the sources.

Whether other cities and regencies in West Sumatra have adopted comparable public-order or anti-LGBT bylaws is not sourced. The OutRight Action International mapping predates the West Sumatra instruments cited here and does not cover the province's newer regulations.
